cards.title: Decide if your product needs a VSL ad before producing one
cards.summary: Use the three qualifying conditions—complex product, low-trust category, or new-to-market category—to decide whether a long educational video ad is worth the production cost.
cards.use_when: Choosing an acquisition creative format for a complicated, distrusted, or brand-new product category, versus running standard short ads.
steps: Qualify your product against the three VSL use cases: (1) complicated products that are hard to explain in a short ad, (2) low-trust categories where the buyer assumes the seller is sketchy, and (3) new categories or new ingredients nobody has heard of.

Check whether your top-of-funnel conversion is capped because customers don't understand the product. If yes, you must educate either in the ad or on the landing page—if not the landing page, then the ad, and the source argues VSLs are the best vehicle for that.
Recognize the production tradeoff: longer VSLs cost more to produce, so start short, learn, then extend. The source warns against jumping straight into a 60-minute script.
If you do not need heavy education to convert, a VSL is not your format—do not adopt it just because it worked for a supplement brand.
Pair the ad with a contextually matched landing page (advertorial or dedicated page), since the source's referenced accounts drove every VSL to a different landing page rather than a generic PDP.
caveats: Qualification is based on the source's stated use cases, not a tested benchmark; the 150% profit lift and low frequency figures are one Australian supplement account's example, not a promise.
Source opinion: VSLs perform better with older demographics, so they may fit your audience differently than a younger one.
cards.source_name: The 7-Part VSL Framework for eCommerce (With Examples).docx

cards.title: The seven-part VSL scripting framework
cards.summary: A repeatable order for scripting a long-form video sales letter: Hook, Problem, Mechanism, Objection Handling, Proof, Risk Reversal, CTA.
cards.use_when: Writing a full VSL ad script for a complex product or low-trust category where doubt must be removed before purchase.
steps: Hook: open with something relevant to the viewer's problem, not a brand introduction.
Problem: state the problem in the customer's own words so the viewer recognizes themselves.
Mechanism: explain why your solution works—in CPG/supplements this is the specific ingredient or technology, not just a claim.
Objection Handling: name the other things the customer tried and explain why those failed, so they don't assume your product will fail the same way.
Proof: product-level evidence (UGC, testimonial, customer count).
Risk Reversal: reduce purchase risk (e.g., a money-back window) before asking for the sale.
CTA: a simple, clear closing ask.
Treat the order as a starting point, not a fixed rule—the source says you don't always script it this way and that the sequence can be reordered.
caveats: Source frames this as a good starting point rather than a universal sequence; it explicitly notes some VSLs work with reordered sections.
A VSL is not a long video for its own sake—the source stresses it's a sales argument that removes doubt in a specific order, and good ones can be as short as 90 seconds.
cards.source_name: The 7-Part VSL Framework for eCommerce (With Examples).docx

cards.title: Hook is the highest-leverage test in a VSL
cards.summary: Because roughly 80% of viewers drop off before the body script starts, test 3–6 hook variations against a fixed body and CTA rather than rewriting everything.
cards.use_when: Improving performance of an already-produced VSL, or structuring a paid social test plan for a long-form video ad.
steps: Build the body of the VSL (problem, mechanism, proof, CTA) first, then produce 3–6 competing hooks against that same body.
Test the hooks as the primary variable rather than rewriting the entire script each time.

Do not bridge immediately into brand or product after the hook—transition into the Problem phase with educational problem-agitation (e.g., explain the biological cause of tooth decay) so viewers stay engaged and don't realize early that it's an ad.

Match hook relevance to audience: the source's strong examples open with content specific to who has the problem (e.g., 'people with tonsil stones'), which filters in the right viewer and lets others self-select out.
Keep the CTA on the main asset if this is your first VSL rather than splitting it into a separate retargeting asset.
caveats: The 80% drop-off figure is the source's stated figure, not a measured benchmark.
The source says many VSLs perform better with older demographics, so readable, large text matters—unreadable text is an editor-level failure it calls out.
cards.source_name: The 7-Part VSL Framework for eCommerce (With Examples).docx

cards.title: Mine real customer data for the objection-handling section
cards.summary: Populate the VSL objection section with verbatim customer reasons for almost-not-buying, drawn from reviews, support tickets, post-purchase surveys, and call recordings.
cards.use_when: Writing the objection-handling portion of a VSL script for a product where buyers considered alternatives or hesitated before purchase.
steps: Pull from reviews, support tickets, post-purchase surveys, and call recordings the reasons people almost didn't buy or what they had already tried.

Map each reason to the script's objection-handling section: name the thing they tried and explain why it didn't work (e.g., gargling only rinses the surface and can't reach the deep biofilm where bacteria live).
Sequence this so the customer feels understood before you introduce the mechanism and product.
Use this miner approach rather than guessing at objections from internal assumptions.
caveats: Source frames this as its own recommended method; it does not provide a validated benchmark for how much objection handling lifts performance.
cards.source_name: The 7-Part VSL Framework for eCommerce (With Examples).docx

cards.title: Use modular editing to cheaply generate VSL variants
cards.summary: Because VSLs are long, you can move whole sections around and cut multiple durations from one asset to produce more creative tests without new shoots.
cards.use_when: Generating multiple creative variations from a single long-form VSL to test on paid social.
steps: After building the full VSL, test reordering sections—e.g., lead with the mechanism before the problem, or pull objection handling earlier. The source reports seeing success moving sections around.
Cut a range of lengths from one script: the source says a 6–10 minute asset can typically be chopped into a 2–3 minute version and a 45-second version by an editor.
Treat length as a variation source rather than the driver of performance—the source believes scripting matters more than length.
Source says length does not have a massive impact on actual performance, so do not over-index on it.
Given a warm viewer who made it through deep ingredient education, push them to a matching landing page rather than a generic PDP.
caveats: Source opinion: length is not the main driver; this is the presenter's view, not a tested law.
Longer production raises cost, so the source recommends starting small.
cards.source_name: The 7-Part VSL Framework for eCommerce (With Examples).docx

cards.title: Bridge from education to product without a premature pitch
cards.summary: Avoid the common mistake of pivoting straight from the intro to a brand/CTA pitch; earn the right to sell by first building the problem and mechanism.
cards.use_when: Drafting the transition from VSL education into the product introduction so viewers don't disengage early.
steps: After the hook, do not cut to a brand or product pitch. Instead move into problem education (e.g., the biological cause of the problem).
Build substantial educational content on the mechanism (in the source's dental example, roughly 30 seconds explaining ingredients and why they work) before presenting the product.
Present the product as the consolidated solution once education has landed—e.g., 'you don't have to source all these ingredients separately; this brand combined them into one.'
Avoid the mistake of stacking claims with no mechanism: too much 'what it is' and not enough 'why it matters' is a listed common failure.
Keep the ad as an educational piece so it doesn't feel like an ad until late in the sequence.
caveats: Source notes some viewers won't tolerate extended mechanism education; it recommends testing a faster version of the same section.
The specific 30-second education length is from one example ad, not a universal target.
cards.source_name: The 7-Part VSL Framework for eCommerce (With Examples).docx

cards.title: Avoid the six common VSL scripting mistakes
cards.summary: A checklist of recurring VSL failures: brand-story hook, claims without mechanism, weak proof, vague offer or missing CTA, and slow pacing or unreadable text.
cards.use_when: Reviewing a drafted VSL script or an underperforming VSL before briefing an editor or relaunching.
steps: Check the hook: a brand story can work as an ad, but source says a VSL is not a brand-story ad—hook with something relevant to the viewer's problem instead. You can weave the founder story into social proof or objection handling later.
Check for mechanism: don't just list what the product does; explain why it works. Claims without mechanism is a listed common mistake.
Check proof: weak or buried proof is a common, easy-to-fix cause of underperformance—surface UGC, testimonials, and customer counts.
Check the offer and CTA: make the offer clear and convincing and include a CTA. The source recommends always including one.
Check pacing and text legibility: slow pacing and small/hard-to-read text are editor-level issues the source says you must be able to spot, especially given VSLs skew toward older viewers.
Add a risk reversal if it's missing—the source criticizes VSLs that skip it.
caveats: Source opinion: 'I recommend you have a CTA'—it is a recommendation, not a proven rule, and the source acknowledges some VSLs run without one.
The source notes an example ad that performed very well despite missing objection handling, so these mistakes are patterns rather than absolute ceilings.
cards.source_name: The 7-Part VSL Framework for eCommerce (With Examples).docx

cards.title: Why some VSLs omit the CTA (and when that's acceptable)
cards.summary: An asset without a CTA is usually an error, but can be deliberate when it feeds an Amazon funnel or a retargeting campaign that handles the close.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to include a CTA on a VSL or whether to run it as top-of-funnel only with a separate retargeting close.
steps: Include a CTA on your primary VSL asset if this is your first—the source recommends it.

If a VSL runs with no CTA, check whether it's pushing traffic to a separate high-converting marketplace (source cites US patterns of running ads or organic content that push people to Amazon, which the source says converts higher than a website landing page).

Or check whether it's a pure top-of-funnel educational asset with retargeting for anyone who watches past a threshold (the source cites retargeting viewers past 25% video views with a hard close), plus natural platform retargeting.
Do not split the CTA out of the VSL on a first attempt—the source says not to complicate the retargeting structure and instead to include the CTA directly.
caveats: The source is explicit that this is its recommendation for beginners, not a universal rule.
The Amazon-funnel and retargeting interpretations are the source's hypotheses for why an example ad lacked a CTA, not confirmed facts about that advertiser.
cards.source_name: The 7-Part VSL Framework for eCommerce (With Examples).docx

cards.title: Pair each VSL with a matching educational landing page
cards.summary: The VSL narrative must continue onto a contextually relevant advertorial or dedicated landing page—dropping to a generic product page breaks continuity and undercuts the ad.
cards.use_when: Setting up the post-click destination for a VSL campaign or running an advertorial/landing page test.
steps: Do not send VSL traffic to a standard PDP with no continuity to what the ad communicated. The source says the VSL won't work if the landing page isn't contextually relevant.
Create a custom landing page (advertorial or dedicated page) per message/angle; the referenced supplement account tied every VSL to a different landing page.
Mirror the ad's mechanism and education on the page so viewers who arrive pre-sold see the story continue rather than restarting.
Make the landing page itself strong, since the source stresses both ad and page quality matter to hold spend.
caveats: Source's account results (aggregated millions, one VSL at ~$360k spend, ROAS ~2.5–3) are examples, not guarantees.
That account made most of its money on second and third purchases (source cites ~150% profit lift after year one), so the VSL's economics depend on your retention, not just first-order ROAS.
cards.source_name: The 7-Part VSL Framework for eCommerce (With Examples).docx

cards.title: Combine UGC, AI animation, and real footage to build VSL B-roll
cards.summary: VSLs stitch together AI UGC, real UGC, and animated motion graphics to explain complex mechanisms without a dedicated shoot.
cards.use_when: Planning the visual production and B-roll sourcing for a long-form educational VSL ad.
steps: Pull together whatever footage and animation ties the story together so you can sustain a long ad without a full shoot.

Use AI video to animate static imagery (e.g., animating a still image of an anatomical process) to create motion graphics for hard-to-shoot technical explanation—the source says this is a very easy way to get B-roll on complex topics.
Mix formats deliberately: the source notes VSLs typically switch between AI UGC, real UGC, and heavy animation.

Watch for stylistic inconsistency—the source criticizes one ad for being too aggressive in using any footage available, coming across as scammy; it recommends keeping branding more consistent (more UGC and less animation, or going all-in on animation).
caveats: The source's 'comes across a little scammy' reaction is a subjective judgment on one ad, not a measured outcome.
Do not read this as an endorsement that more animation always performs—the source pushes for consistency.
cards.source_name: The 7-Part VSL Framework for eCommerce (With Examples).docx

cards.title: Read performance signals: likes, launch age, and frequency
cards.summary: Use public engagement and launch age as rough signals of a VSL's spend level, and frequency as a rough indicator of how cold an ad still is.
cards.use_when: Sourcing winning VSL examples for creative inspiration or assessing whether an ad is still reaching new audiences.
steps: Treat like count and launch age as a rough proxy for lifetime spend—the source cites an ad with ~25,000 likes launched roughly 2 months prior as having spent at least $100k.
Track frequency as an indicator of how cold the ad is and how well it is moving into new audiences, especially in the current platform era the source calls 'post-Andromeda.'

Contextualize frequency against market size: holding large spend at very low frequency in a small market (the source cites Australia) is notable, while the US can support similar spend at lower frequency because the population is far larger.
Remember the source's point that a low first-order ROAS (~2.5–3) can still be highly profitable when retention drives most of the revenue on later purchases.
caveats: These are rough heuristics from public ad observations, not verified spend data or benchmarks.
The source explicitly says ROAS and scaling rules belong in analytics/performance, not creative—use these signals for creative sourcing, not as performance targets.
cards.source_name: The 7-Part VSL Framework for eCommerce (With Examples).docx

cards.title: Recognize when a VSL script can reorder its sections
cards.summary: The seven-part order is a template, not a fixed sequence—the source's working example moves problem before hook education and mechanism after objection handling.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to keep or reorder the standard VSL section flow when scripting a new creative.
steps: Use the standard order (Hook → Problem → Mechanism → Objection Handling → Proof → Risk Reversal → CTA) as a default starting point.
Consider reordering if it serves the audience: the source's tonsil-stone example ran Hook → Problem → Objection Handling → Mechanism, and the source calls this valid rather than wrong.
Consider pulling problem agitation forward if the hook is ingredient-heavy—the source says it would test moving the agitation earlier in the dental example.
Test reordered versions as modular variations of the same asset rather than writing entirely new scripts.
Keep the elements intact even when reordering: the dental example skipped objection handling and the source flagged that gap as something to add in future versions.
caveats: The source says reordering is situational and the default order is a starting point, not a universal requirement.
Reordering evidence in the source is observational (the source's own notes on ads it reviewed), not a controlled test result.
cards.source_name: The 7-Part VSL Framework for eCommerce (With Examples).docx
